#Uranium $MYRUF $M.CN

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. Myriad now owns Copper Mountain outright and can use that work to choose where a new hole will tell it the most. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

The October 28 update gives a sense of what they’re finding. At Hesitation, one hole returned 34.3 metres at 399 ppm eU₃O₈ in preliminary downhole gamma readings. I’m watching the lab assays next.

Then there’s what Myriad picked up in Argentina. On November 2, it announced the acquisition of Los Altares, roughly 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district. The price was C$300,000 in cash, C$700,000 in shares and a 2% royalty. That works out to about C$18 per hectare up front, including the shares, on ground with roughly 12,500 metres of reported historical drilling.

That’s why I like Myriad’s chances if the sector rebound holds. Argentina took a modest bite out of the treasury, while the drilling in Wyoming could give investors something worth repricing the stock for: a first modern estimate of how many pounds Copper Mountain holds.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Myriad Uranium. Please do your own research.

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. Myriad now owns Copper Mountain outright and can use that work to choose where a new hole will tell it the most. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

The October 28 update gives a sense of what they’re finding. At Hesitation, one hole returned 34.3 metres at 399 ppm eU₃O₈ in preliminary downhole gamma readings. I’m watching the lab assays next.

Then there’s what Myriad picked up in Argentina. On November 2, it announced the acquisition of Los Altares, roughly 55,000 hectares in the Cerro Solo uranium district. The price was C$300,000 in cash, C$700,000 in shares and a 2% royalty. That works out to about C$18 per hectare up front, including the shares, on ground with roughly 12,500 metres of reported historical drilling.

That’s why I like Myriad’s chances if the sector rebound holds. Argentina took a modest bite out of the treasury, while the drilling in Wyoming could give investors something worth repricing the stock for: a first modern estimate of how many pounds Copper Mountain holds.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. 𝗜𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗺𝗯𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

GeneDx is a leader in pediatric genomic diagnostics. The company helps diagnose rare genetic diseases in children, sometimes ending years of uncertainty for families who have been going from one hospital to another looking for answers.

𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗞𝗘𝗘𝗣 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗧 𝗔𝗡 𝗘𝗫𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘.

The demand is already there. GeneDx reported 25% year-over-year growth in exome and genome testing volumes in Q3, with full-year growth guidance of at least 28%. More doctors are ordering genomic tests, more patients are being diagnosed, and the clinical value of this technology is becoming increasingly clear.

But here is the problem.

𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.

Approximately 48% of its insured outpatient testing volume comes from Medicaid patients, yet whole genome sequencing is covered by Medicaid in only 25 states.

Think about this for a moment. You have a company with rapidly growing demand for its services, but the payment system has not caught up with the technology.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗦𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚.

If passed as described, it would make qualifying pediatric genomic sequencing a mandatory Medicaid benefit, allow doctors to use it as a first-tier diagnostic test, and require separate payment for hospital testing.

This is not simply about increasing the number of tests.

It is about changing the economics of tests GeneDx is already performing, while potentially opening the door to many more patients.

Today, every additional test creates clinical value, but it does not necessarily translate into money collected.

With broader coverage and a clearer reimbursement framework, growing testing volumes could finally translate into growing cash collections.

And that is a completely different business.

Imagine a company growing testing volumes by 25% annually while struggling to get paid. Now imagine the same company with broader reimbursement, better collection rates, and a much larger addressable market.

Revenue growth could accelerate without requiring an equivalent increase in testing volume. Fixed costs could be spread across more paid tests, improving margins and potentially cash flow.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵. 𝗜𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀.

Of course, coverage does not guarantee payment. Reimbursement rates, implementation, and GeneDx’s own execution would still matter.

𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗧𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗔𝗗𝗩𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘.

GeneDx has built a database from hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of genetic and clinical data points.

Sequencing DNA is becoming cheap. Understanding which mutations actually cause disease is much harder.

Without enough patient data, you cannot connect the dots.

You can buy sequencing machines, hire scientists, and build laboratories. What you cannot easily buy is years of accumulated clinical knowledge.

Every additional patient potentially strengthens that database, making it even harder for competitors to replicate.

This is the real moat of $WGS.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. 𝗜𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗺𝗯𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

GeneDx is a leader in pediatric genomic diagnostics. The company helps diagnose rare genetic diseases in children, sometimes ending years of uncertainty for families who have been going from one hospital to another looking for answers.

𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗞𝗘𝗘𝗣 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗧 𝗔𝗡 𝗘𝗫𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘.

The demand is already there. GeneDx reported 25% year-over-year growth in exome and genome testing volumes in Q3, with full-year growth guidance of at least 28%. More doctors are ordering genomic tests, more patients are being diagnosed, and the clinical value of this technology is becoming increasingly clear.

But here is the problem.

Approximately 48% of its insured outpatient testing volume comes from Medicaid patients, yet whole genome sequencing is covered by Medicaid in only 25 states.

Think about this for a moment. You have a company with rapidly growing demand for its services, but the payment system has not caught up with the technology.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗦𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚.

If passed as described, it would make qualifying pediatric genomic sequencing a mandatory Medicaid benefit, allow doctors to use it as a first-tier diagnostic test, and require separate payment for hospital testing.

This is not simply about increasing the number of tests.

It is about changing the economics of tests GeneDx is already performing, while potentially opening the door to many more patients.

Today, every additional test creates clinical value, but it does not necessarily translate into money collected.

With broader coverage and a clearer reimbursement framework, growing testing volumes could finally translate into growing cash collections.

And that is a completely different business.

Imagine a company growing testing volumes by 25% annually while struggling to get paid. Now imagine the same company with broader reimbursement, better collection rates, and a much larger addressable market.

Revenue growth could accelerate without requiring an equivalent increase in testing volume. Fixed costs could be spread across more paid tests, improving margins and potentially cash flow.

Of course, coverage does not guarantee payment. Reimbursement rates, implementation, and GeneDx’s own execution would still matter.

GeneDx has built a database from hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of genetic and clinical data points.

Sequencing DNA is becoming cheap. Understanding which mutations actually cause disease is much harder.

Without enough patient data, you cannot connect the dots.

You can buy sequencing machines, hire scientists, and build laboratories. What you cannot easily buy is years of accumulated clinical knowledge.

Every additional patient potentially strengthens that database, making it even harder for competitors to replicate.

This is the real moat of $WGS.

Approximately 48% of its insured outpatient testing volume comes from Medicaid patients, yet whole genome sequencing is covered by Medicaid in only 25 states.

Think about this for a moment. You have a company with rapidly growing demand for its services, but the payment system has not caught up with the technology.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗟𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗦𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗟𝗗 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗚.

If passed as described, it would make qualifying pediatric genomic sequencing a mandatory Medicaid benefit, allow doctors to use it as a first-tier diagnostic test, and require separate payment for hospital testing.

This is not simply about increasing the number of tests.

It is about changing the economics of tests GeneDx is already performing, while potentially opening the door to many more patients.

Today, every additional test creates clinical value, but it does not necessarily translate into money collected.

With broader coverage and a clearer reimbursement framework, growing testing volumes could finally translate into growing cash collections.

And that is a completely different business.

Imagine a company growing testing volumes by 25% annually while struggling to get paid. Now imagine the same company with broader reimbursement, better collection rates, and a much larger addressable market.

Revenue growth could accelerate without requiring an equivalent increase in testing volume. Fixed costs could be spread across more paid tests, improving margins and potentially cash flow.

Of course, coverage does not guarantee payment. Reimbursement rates, implementation, and GeneDx’s own execution would still matter.

𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗧𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗘 𝗔𝗗𝗩𝗔𝗡𝗧𝗔𝗚𝗘.

GeneDx has built a database from hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of genetic and clinical data points.

Sequencing DNA is becoming cheap. Understanding which mutations actually cause disease is much harder.

Without enough patient data, you cannot connect the dots.

You can buy sequencing machines, hire scientists, and build laboratories. What you cannot easily buy is years of accumulated clinical knowledge.

Every additional patient potentially strengthens that database, making it even harder for competitors to replicate.

This is the real moat of $WGS.

𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗞 𝗔𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗖𝗞.

$WGS traded near $100 just a few months ago, when investors were hoping its financial performance would improve. Today it trades around $46.

Corvex Management and Casdin Capital maintained their reported positions through Q3, even when the stock was trading near $100. Deep Track Capital, another specialist healthcare fund, recently disclosed approximately 6% ownership.

These are investors with considerable experience in the industry.

My thesis is that the market has been valuing GeneDx as a company with strong clinical demand but serious problems turning that demand into cash.

𝗜𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲 𝗮 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.

That combination could justify a significant re-rating.

The bill is not guaranteed to pass, and GeneDx still has serious operational problems to solve. But the potential change in its economics is enormous.

I cannot imagine that 10 years from now, parents will still spend years going from hospital to hospital trying to understand what is wrong with their children when the technology already exists to provide answers much earlier.

hype bought back:

> 90 days before the top: 2.31M

> november: ~36K a day, the most since march

> hype at the top: $33

That isn't what End to End encryption means. 

It just means the payload is encrypted on the user's machine, it can travel across several intermediaries until it reaches the endpoint (i.e., privy's servers). 

It is then decrypted by the recipient. 

Importantly, it should _also_ be authenticated, so when the user encrypts the message they know the public key indeed belongs to the recipient (i.e., privy) and not anyone else.
